title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Landscaping
audience: Landscaping business owners who set prices or plan monthly revenue, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a landscaping business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level a landscaping business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. The figure helps you set prices, decide when to add a crew and check whether a new service can pay for itself. Project income is lumpy, so the calculation is only as good as the monthly average behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of projects. They include the vehicle and trailer loans, insurance, phone and software subscriptions, yard or storage rent, and any plant hire agreement paid monthly regardless of use. Variable costs move with each project. They include materials not on-charged, subcontractor fees, fuel, consumables and the card payment fees charged on each sale. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025). Check the percentage across at least three periods before relying on it.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. One minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 30 per cent becomes 0.30. The contribution margin of a 30 per cent variable cost is then 0.70 (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source, period and date. Compute the contribution margin, then divide the fixed costs by it. Convert the result into a number of projects at your average project price, and round up to whole projects, because a part project does not cover costs on its own (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Check that the average is what you actually charge, excluding GST if you are registered. GST is added to the price once a business is registered, and the threshold is $75,000 of GST turnover (ATO, 14 September 2026). Do not use a published range as the average: the Melbourne cost guide's garden design or plan runs from $720 to $4,500, and that range says nothing about your own project mix (What's the Damage, verified 1 November 2026).

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit, and that the price is stated on the same GST basis as the sales. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set a price.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average project price, excluding GST if registered, to get the number of projects needed each month, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: Hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not market data: a two-person landscaping business has fixed costs of $6,000 a month (vehicle and trailer loans, insurance, software and a yard), variable costs of 30 per cent of sales (materials not on-charged, subcontractors, fuel and card fees) and an average project price of $3,000 excluding GST.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many projects must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.30, which is 0.70. Break-even revenue is $6,000 divided by 0.70, which is $8,571.43 a month. At $3,000 a project that is 2.86 projects, so the business needs 3 projects to cover its costs. Each project contributes $2,100 ($3,000 multiplied by 0.70). Check the arithmetic: two projects contribute $4,200, which leaves $1,800 short of the $6,000 fixed costs, and three projects contribute $6,300. Before setting prices, the business checks that the 30 per cent includes every variable cost, that $6,000 is a monthly figure, and that $3,000 is the average project price actually charged, excluding GST.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months
Project invoice log with dates and GST status

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

commonErrors.error: Using a single large project as the average
commonErrors.prevention: Average the project price over at least three months of invoices, so one large or small project does not set the figure.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs and GST registration with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.
This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Licence and registration rules for landscaping work are separate and are not covered here.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period, GST basis and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period and one GST basis throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $6,000 a month and variable costs are 30% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same landscaping business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel

sourceReferences: Xero Australia, 'Break-even point formula' glossary entry, https://www.xero.com/au/glossary/break-even-point-formula/, dated 23 July 2026. Supports: contribution margin is price minus variable cost; break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio; job counts are rounded up to whole jobs.

ANZ, 'Setting the right price for your product or service', https://www.anz.com.au/business/business-hub/starting-business/start/setting-the-right-price-for-your-product-or-service/, dated 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025. Supports: definitions of fixed and variable costs; costs must be covered to avoid operating at a loss.

ATO, 'Registering for GST', https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/gst-excise-and-indirect-taxes/gst/registering-for-gst, last updated 14 September 2026. Supports: GST turnover threshold of $75,000; GST is added to the price once registered.

What's the Damage, 'Landscaping cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/landscaping-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026. Cost guide; not a regulator. Supports: garden design or plan $720 / $1,800 / $4,500. Used only to show the range is not an average for one business.
